newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO beset by problems as it tries to find new role.
newsitem.headline: NATO beset by problems as it tries to find new role.

text.p: Plans by NATO to forge a new security order in Europe have become beset by two embarrassing internal squabbles as the alliance seeks to present a united front on issues from Bosnia to relations with Russia.

If differences between Paris and Washington and between Athens and Ankara are not contained, they could threaten NATO's structural reforms, its plans for a European defence identity and possibly even its enlargement into eastern Europe.
"We really must, before we enlarge, get our own house in order," one NATO official said.

Both disputes concern the 16-nation North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's attempts to create a greater security role for its European nations, a move eagerly sought by the European Union and welcomed in America.
Row One involves the United States and France.

As part of its watershed decision to rejoin NATO's military structure, France has said it wants more Europeans in senior commands. It has specifically set its eyes on the job of commander of southern European forces (AFSOUTH) based in Naples.
Washington insists the job should remain, as it always has, in American hands -- in part because it is the United States's main post for influencing the Middle East militarily.

Although French Prime Minister Alain Juppe said on Tuesday he believed there was a way around the problem, senior officials at NATO say there is an impasse and that it is blocking agreement on a new overall command structure.
NATO is trying to cut back its commands to make it leaner and more efficient as it adapts to life after the Cold War.
France has said it will not come back fully into NATO's military structure unless it is satisfied with the alliance's Europeanisation.
Paris has not said it will block enlargement if it does not get what it wants. But it clearly believes it could.
"This point too requires an agreement," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said on Tuesday when asked in Paris about the opening of enlargement negotiations.
Row Two involves Turkey and Greece, two old rivals whose disagreements have blocked a number of NATO and EU policies.

At a Western European Union (WEU) meeting in Ostend, Belgium, on Tuesday, Turkey threatened to veto the use of NATO equipment by the WEU because Greece had objected to Ankara being given a strong role in deciding WEU missions.
Turkey, along with Norway and Iceland, is only an associate member of the WEU, but a full member of NATO.
Greece, a full member of both groups, had objected to a WEU proposal to require an unanimous decision to launch a mission by the 10 full WEU members and the three associates.
"I explained that Europe needs Turkey more than Turkey needs Europe," Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller told the Anatolian news agency.

If carried out, the threat would unravel one of the new NATO's much-heralded policies -- that of allowing its European members, through the WEU, to conduct peacekeeping and humaitarian aid efforts on their own but with NATO material.
Officials said the two rows become linked at this point, because the United States argues that having an American in charge of NATO's southern command keeps Greek and Turkish rivalries in check.

NATO officials say both rows stem from the fact that the alliance is in a state of change, shifting gear from being a static military command facing a large enemy to being a more fluid organisation dealing with diverse situations.
It is also because the old enemy, the Soviet Union, is not longer there to concentrate the mind.
